brief.head: Words nobody opposes
brief.text: Nobody can be seen to favour money laundering or terrorist financing, Ajay Shah said. Under those words India built a surveillance system that drags households through endless KYC. {071-C19}

brief.head: Rule-maker, cop, judge
brief.text: Indian regulators write the rules, enforce them and rule on violations, Ajay Shah said; India is the only country where regulators also judge. The result is a climate of fear. {071-C15}

brief.head: Finance as the brain
brief.text: Finance is the brain of the economy, Ajay Shah said, so the best minds belong there; working in a financial firm instead of doing particle physics is no misallocation. {071-C16}

brief.head: Why Marx feels natural
brief.text: Amit Varma argued that Marx’s ideas will always resonate more than Hayek’s, because they flatter instincts for top-down planning, zero-sum thinking and a strongman for the tribe. {071-C05}

brief.head: Not Pitroda’s doing
brief.text: Amit Varma dismissed the story that Sam Pitroda made India’s telecom revolution happen. “This is rubbish,” he said: markets and the Vajpayee-era reforms did it. {071-J24}

thought.text: Capitalism without failure is socialism for the rich.

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah and Amit Varma on India’s money since 1947
lead.head: The planners never left the bank
body: For Ajay Shah, the journey of Indian finance since 1947 comes down to one diagnosis: “an intellectual failure of the Indian elite to build the knowledge and community around words like market failure, central planning, rule of law, state capability”. {071-C06}
Shah told the story as a chapter for a Cambridge history of modern South Asia. Amit Varma called it “the definitive work on the subject”.

It starts with central planning. If the government decides products and processes, Shah said, that is central planning, and after independence banking became one extended planning system. Delhi licensed the steel mill; Bombay’s bureaucracy supplied the credit.
“The RBI became the central planning shop of the financial sector,” he said.

Officials spoke unembarrassed of resource mobilisation: taking households’ money and giving it to “our chosen ones”. A one-size-fits-all bureaucracy, Shah argued, serves only the top income decile. “You are harming the interests of ninety percent of India,” he said. {071-C02}
## Stars and laggards

Banking stayed a disappointment. After decades of failing to learn bank regulation and resolution, Shah would rather India did not bet on a large banking system, and grew finance through bond markets, NBFCs and foreign banks instead.
“If we are a third world country and we don’t know how to run air traffic control, then maybe you should not have so much air travel,” he said. {071-C04}
The equity market was the star pupil. SEBI, NSE and the depository NSDL, built from the late 1980s to the mid-1990s, made what Shah called one of the great success stories of the Indian reforms.

Mutual funds came out reasonably well. Insurance was mediocre, pensions saw major reversals, and capital controls survived the reforms: FEMA, which replaced FERA in 1999, begins by banning all transactions.
## Who looks after a reform?

Why did the good reforms fade? Shah’s answer is knowledge and community. The equity reforms were carried by a team across the finance ministry, SEBI, NSE and academic institutions, who argued in blogs, op-eds and seminars.
When that team was broken up, he said, the community was thrown away and India went back to “a normal bumbling world of policymaking”. {071-C17}
Pension reform withered out of inattention. Inflation targeting, he warned, could be next, with many on the left back to sniping at it.
The hosts parted ways over bailouts. Varma, who wants the state never to bail anyone out, told Shah: “To me, you are a lefty.”
## Three phases
Shah sees three phases: explicit socialism from 1947 to 1991; then, until perhaps 2016, real knowledge-building mixed with exuberant labels; and now a muddle.

Throughout, India has practised isomorphic mimicry, building institutions that look right from outside. “You can show a gullible foreign visitor that oh we have a bond market,” he said. Officials still effectively set every interest rate. {071-C18}
His own views have moved. The young Shah cheered press releases; the older one reads the laws, and finds the devil in implementation, the land of public choice, state capability and rule of law.
The task now, he said, is a 25-year journey of building knowledge and building community.
Varma ended by recommending the paper, and its author, a man once “greatly respected by all as an economist, till he turned a YouTuber and started doing content”.

second.label: Banks and computers
second.head: Disk by decree
second.deck: How an RBI committee wrote the IT strategy of every bank in India
body: When computers arrived in the early 1990s, the Reserve Bank of India decided that banks needed computerisation. The Rangarajan Committee then wrote down exactly what every bank had to do, Ajay Shah said. {071-S01}

It named the CPU and the disk controller: an SMD controller, for Uniplus Unix machines with Motorola 68K processors. “You could literally take the RBI report and it became the IT strategy of every bank,” Shah said.

Nobody was embarrassed, because prescribing technology was seen as RBI’s job. For Shah, officials picking winners is “a complete red line”. Amit Varma saw the same mindset in a single state-backed payment system today. {#dpi}

quote.text: They chose the name of the CPU. They chose the name of the disc controller which will be inside every bank.

second.caption: the Rangarajan Committee’s hardware

third.head: Credit comes to the cinema
body: Ajay Shah was in the audience at an Indian Express event with KV Kamath and Mukesh Ambani on stage. Shekhar Gupta asked Ambani what he had seen change over the reform years.
In the bad old days, Ambani said, his driver had to come to him for a loan. {071-S13} Recently, when he went to watch a movie at Metro, a teenager plucked his sleeve and asked if he wanted one.

Household credit, Shah said, is one of the real successes of Indian finance. Credit bureaus changed borrowers’ incentives by recording defaults, and private NBFCs took loans to households across the country.

Amit Varma passed on a worry, from Harsh Vardhan among others, that consumer credit had exploded unsustainably. Shah called the recent debt-fuelled spell “a small glitch in a larger journey”. {#glitch}
third.caption: the loan at the movies

p2.title: Five parts, one flaw
p2.deck: Banks, markets, borders, bankruptcy and crises: Ajay Shah’s account of Indian finance since 1947, argued over with Amit Varma

sections.label: Banking
sections.head: One little super bank
sections.caption: banking as central planning
body: Indian banking was nationalised in stages, from SBI to the sweeps of 1969 and 1980. Ajay Shah traced the idea to the 1848 *Communist Manifesto*, which called for credit centralised in a state monopoly bank. “Some academic scribbler in the years gone by shapes the madman in frenzy,” he said. {071-J02}
Each gap in the planned system got a new public sector monopoly: IDBI, ICICI, HDFC. Shah would have let a hundred business models compete and ninety-five go bust.
By the early 1990s, he said, RBI had realised that banking regulation existed and that it knew nothing about it. A Rs 5,500 crore hole found inside Indian Bank in 1995 started the learning. {071-S02}
## Two things to get right

Regulation, Shah said, comes down to two things. Value loans honestly: if a loan of 100 would fetch 80 at auction today, book the 20 loss now. And hold enough equity. Indian banks run about five of equity against 95 of deposits, too thin for India’s volatile economy, and a ratio that made bribery pay at family-run banks, most of which failed. {071-C03}
Honest valuation drags bad news into the open, which a planner resists. “In a central planning system, RBI is mother,” Shah said. “Mother cannot allow bad news to be told to the public.” {071-J03}
~ Since 1992, about five per cent of one year’s GDP has gone as government money to the public sector banks: credit underpriced, Shah said, and paid for by the taxpayer. {#gdp5}

quote.text: It is too easy to give out loans of hundred and take bribes of ten.

sections.label: Equity markets
sections.head: Trucks full of paper
sections.caption: the stock market reforms
body: The Bombay Stock Exchange, run by a club of mostly Gujarati and Marwari brokers, did little after independence. Yet India had had the first stock market of Asia, Ajay Shah said, in 1874. {#bse1874}

The club could not settle trades on a predictable clock, and some members were hand in glove with market manipulators. Shah is still troubled that its 300 to 400 brokers never struck a deal among themselves to modernise their own exchange. {071-C07}
So the state stepped in, with SEBI from 1988, NSE from 1992 and the depository NSDL from 1995.
## Software needed shares

The new market mattered most to new industries. Banks would not lend to early software firms, which had no factory to pledge. Shah draws a direct line from the Infosys IPO of 1994 to NSE and SEBI. {071-S04}

The old system had choked on small sums. In August and September 1993, foreign money began arriving at about $100 million a month, and the streets of Bombay filled with “truckloads of share certificates”. {071-S05}
~ Shah ranks the equity market alongside the telecom reforms and Major General Khanduri’s National Highways Authority as heroes of the reform era. That team, he said, has since been broken up.

quote.text: Why were these people not able to come together and find a Coasian bargain and do that negotiation between themselves

sections.label: Currency controls
sections.head: Money that may not leave
sections.caption: capital controls
body: In the first globalisation there were no capital controls, Ajay Shah said, and bond issues in London built India’s railways. Then the British imposed currency restrictions in 1939, and Indira Gandhi amended the 1947 foreign exchange law in 1973 to add criminal consequences. {#fera1973}
Shah treats the freedom to move wealth as a human right: leaving a country, as a Jewish refugee left Germany, means little if your wealth stays trapped.

The economics is just as plain. Capital is the biggest cost in a ton of steel, bigger than iron ore or coal, and spreading investments worldwide lowers risk. “The dream of economics is that you, Amit Bhai, should own a flat in Tokyo that you rent to a Japanese guy,” Shah told Amit Varma. {071-C08}
## A law that starts with no

FEMA, the 1999 law that replaced FERA, begins by banning all transactions. In 1993, when India announced current account convertibility, the young Shah cheered; years later he read the laws and found it did not exist. {071-S09}
In practice, those who can pay lawyers and accountants get openness, and everybody else is shut out. Varma called it a classic case of the lack of freedom hurting the poor first. {071-C09}
~ Varma wanted a Foreign Exchange Freedom Act instead. Of “regulation” and “management”, Shah said: “I don’t know which word is more offensive.” {071-J07}

quote.text: This is a classic illustration of how the lack of freedom always hurts the poor first.

sections.label: Bankruptcy
sections.head: Ice cubes melt, so hurry
sections.caption: bankruptcy and the melting ice cube
body: Firms must be able to fail, Ajay Shah said, or there is no real competition. The question is whether they fail badly, in a power play where “the person with the most gundas grabs assets”, or by a predictable script that everyone signs up to in advance. {071-C10}

He offered a magic pair of ideas. When a firm fails, the loss has already happened: if 100 of capital is now worth 40, the only question is who gets the 40. And a firm in distress melts, as vendors go unpaid, machines go unmaintained and staff walk away. {071-C11}
## Never repossessed

India had little of this. In the late 1990s Deepak Parekh, head of HDFC, told Shah that it had never repossessed a house. Lenders got the power to seize collateral only with SARFAESI in 2002. {071-S11}

The bankruptcy code began when KP Krishnan took a section of the 2015 budget speech to Arun Jaitley and suggested blowing it up into a full code. TK Viswanathan led the committee; Shah and Susan were members, and Susan led the drafting. {071-S12}
The result has been lukewarm, Shah said: RBI steers banks away from the code, implementation has faltered at IBBI and NCLT, and the reform community dispersed.
~ Shah quoted Hemingway: asked how he went bankrupt, a character answers, “slowly at first and then suddenly”. {071-J20}

quote.text: So you want to recognize that speed is of essence because a firm going into death is a melting ice cube.

sections.label: Systemic risk
sections.head: Crises, made in India
sections.caption: crises made at home
body: Ajay Shah used to think of systemic crises as global shocks: Asia in 1997, LTCM, 2008. Now he says “the Indian financial system is entirely capable of generating a systemic crisis all on its own”. {071-C13}

Three failures interact, he said: monetary policy that is not inflation targeting, weak prudential regulation, and no way to shut failed firms. The central bank ends up “pouring LSD in the punch when the party gets going”. {071-J11}
His paper finds six systemic crises from 1992 to 2018, among them Andhra Pradesh’s 2010 ban on microfinance. {#sixcrises}
Shah even found Indian money in Oscar Wilde’s *The Importance of Being Earnest*, from 1895: “The chapter on the fall of the rupee you may omit.” {071-J19}
## To bail or not
At any moment, Shah said, regulators are good at fighting the last war. Clever people optimise around every rule, so some crises are a price worth paying for the growth finance brings. {071-C12}
Amit Varma disagreed. Bailouts privatise profits and socialise losses, he said, and every one is a tax on the poor; the state should never bail anyone out.
Shah partly conceded. In many, many things, he said, the correct answer is to let go and take moral hazard seriously.
~ Varma had just called him a lefty. Shah’s reply: “You are a man after my own heart.”

quote.text: If there is systemic risk, let the fricking system fail so the next time it doesn’t happen.

side.boxText: Ajay Shah’s Table 2, a one-page chronology of milestones across every sector, is the part everybody loves, he says. The paper began as a chapter for *The Cambridge Economic History of Modern South Asia*, and Amit Varma calls it “almost a magisterial account”. {071-R01}

contQuote.text: And that entire team was disrupted and we’ve thrown away that community, we’ve thrown away that team, and we’re really back to a normal bumbling world of policymaking and then many things start going wrong.

p3.title: Tales of the reform years
p3.deck: A keystroke, a payphone, a green line and a bankruptcy nobody noticed

stories.start: And I also remember how uh N STL was inaugurated on the sixth
stories.end: that was the end of the ceremony. So the entire ceremony was five minutes.
stories.caption: the five-minute launch of NSDL
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah remembers the day the depository opened
stories.head: Five minutes, years in the making
body: In August and September 1993, the first surge of foreign investment reached India at about $100 million a month. The Bombay Stock Exchange choked on it, and trucks carried paper share certificates through the streets. {#hundredmillion}

Foreign investors could not work with that. Part of the answer was NSDL, a stock depository, and it needed an enabling law: the Depositories Act, “a beautiful law”, Ajay Shah said, drafted by PJ Nayak and M Sahu.
But it had to pass Parliament, and the government of the day did not have a majority.

Help came from an unlikely quarter. The British Chancellor of the Exchequer met Manmohan Singh and raised the law as a real choke point. Singh, in turn, pressed the Congress political establishment to get it through by hook or by crook. “I don’t know what means were applied,” Shah said, “but they got that law through.”

On 6 November 1996, Shah was in the auditorium at Nehru Centre for the inauguration. On stage, as he remembers it, were Bimal Jalan, the RBI governor; DR Mehta, the SEBI chairman; CB Bhave, the depository’s MD; and P Chidambaram.
Somebody pressed one carriage return to pretend that a first transaction had taken place. Chidambaram hugged Bhave. “So the entire ceremony was five minutes,” Shah said. {071-S06}
~ He counts it among the happiest days of his life. The whole tale, Amit Varma said, is told at greater length in their ten-and-a-half-hour episode of *The Seen and the Unseen*.
stories.why: Big institutional change looks tiny on the day it arrives. Behind one keystroke lay years of drafting, persuasion and political deal-making by a small group of people: the knowledge and community Shah calls the real engine of reform. {071-C17}
stories.postscript: Told it was one of Shah’s happiest days, Amit Varma replied: “It’s so easy to make you happy.” {071-J04}

stories.start: And one of the best counterpoints to that Attachment for socialism
stories.end: as telecom as a bureaucracy or steel as a bureaucracy or what have you
stories.caption: the village payphone
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on what telecom shows about banking
stories.head: One payphone, every village
body: Telecom was once as tidy as Indian banking, Ajay Shah said: a government monopoly of the Department of Telecommunications, MTNL, BSNL and VSNL, defended in the name of national security. The rich got phones after a ten-year wait or a bribe. Most of India got none.
The official dream was a village telephone scheme: one payphone in every village, where you threw in a coin, made one call and could not call long distance. {071-S03}

Then Sudhindra Kulkarni and Arun Shourie, working in the Vajpayee government, opened the sector to private and foreign players. Mobile calls that once cost sixteen rupees a minute became a “janta product”, and India now has about 1.1 billion telephones for 1.4 billion people. {#telephones}
~ Banking, Shah said, missed out on all that energy. Run as a bureaucracy, it stayed exactly as dead as telecom had been.
stories.why: A bureaucratic monopoly serves only the elite, while competition reaches the whole country. Telecom, for Shah, is the counterfactual for nationalised banking, whose one-size-fits-all design served only the top decile. {071-C02}

stories.start: I want to tell a story from Maggie Thatcher.
stories.end: in the future no lefty will be able to bring back the capital controls
stories.caption: Thatcher and the green line
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how Britain locked in capital freedom
stories.head: Thatcher rubs out the green line
body: When Margaret Thatcher’s Britain opened its current and capital accounts, Ajay Shah said, some people proposed a compromise: free everything, but make people submit some data.

You would stand in a queue, submit a form and get automatic access to a green line. The reformers refused. Keep the reporting, they argued, and a future government could easily shut the gate again. “The point is to destroy the green line,” Shah said.
So in the early 1980s Britain removed the reporting requirements too, “so that in the future no lefty will be able to bring back the capital controls”. {071-S08}
~ India did the opposite. It kept its apparatus of control when FEMA replaced FERA, and sure enough, in 2015 the criminal clauses came back. {#criminal2015}
stories.why: Reforms must be built to be hard to reverse. Leave the forms and the queue in place, Shah’s story suggests, and a later government will find it easy to switch the controls back on.
stories.postscript: Amit Varma’s favourite story: at her first cabinet meeting, Thatcher threw down Hayek’s *The Constitution of Liberty* and said, “This is what we believe in.” {071-J22}

stories.start: And the greatest, greatest example of this nature is what happened
stories.end: That's the dream of bankruptcy, that some firms are worthy of rescuing.
stories.caption: the bankruptcy nobody noticed
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how Europe’s telecom firms failed quietly
stories.head: Bust, without a dropped call
body: European telecom firms were over-optimistic about the 2G auctions, Ajay Shah said, and bid ridiculous sums of money for spectrum licences. The revenue never came, and the firms went bankrupt.
Their customers noticed nothing. “Our phones continued to work, our phone numbers stayed,” Shah said. “We never got a missed call. We never got a dropped call.” {071-S10}
Somewhere up in the financial superstructure, the old shareholders and bondholders took the losses, and new shareholders picked up the firms as going concerns.
~ In India, Shah said, the years go by and the firm is destroyed before anything happens. Caught early, he argued, perhaps 80 or 90 per cent of firms would be worth saving. {#ninety}

quote.text: That’s the dream of bankruptcy, that some firms are worthy of rescuing.
